I should preface this by saying I will probably be touching on some of the same points that were made during the review of Dunkirk by the Death Panel on TDS. But that said, even listening to their analysis of the movie didn't prepare me for what I saw. There may be spoilers, as I am writing this while on my second glass of rum.

For starters, it's an absolute no brainer as to why the kikes have universally hated this movie. It's not about them. It's about Us.

It's a movie that doesn't depict epic battles of good versus evil, of the struggle of Allied forces against the evil Axis, nor of the fictitious plight of the kikes. It doesn't demonize Adolf Hitler as some raving drug-crazed lunatic, it doesn't paint the NatSoc German Soldiers as insecure, angry white men with annoyingly high pitched voices, and it doesn't ever once even use the word Nazi.

What does it depict? Honor, courage, dedication, integrity, strength, duty, self-sacrifice, an indomitable fighting spirit, in a word, Patriotism. It highlights all of the best qualities of our kind, our race, our People, in a way very few films ever have, ever will, or ever might do. It highlights what we, the mere mortal men, can accomplish with but an ounce of steel to our souls, however small that accomplishment might be. It shows that the bravery of one person can change the outcome of so many lives, save so many souls from the cold grasp of death.

With Tommy the soldier, we see the will to survive, to face death and persevere. Time and again he comes within a hairs breadth of gunfire, bombs and the works. And while some would look at his repeated attempts to leave the beach ahead of his comrades, it isn't something we look at with disdain. It is a stark reminder of the horrific nature of war, of battles with our fellow men. Very few, dare I say none, would pass up the chance to escape such a living hell for the sake of camaraderie and solidarity.

Despite this, he tries - ultimately in vain - to stay by the side of a French soldier posing as an English troop, in hopes to escape. He puts his own neck on the line when his fellow Brits try to turn on the frenchie. But despite everything, he carries on. The indomitable fighting spirit of the Anglo - of indeed the White man - is perfectly captured with him.

With Mr. Dawson, his son Peter and his son's friend George, we find the courage rarely seen in peoples outside of the armed forces. Instead of letting the British Royal Navy commandeer his vessel, Mr. Dawson chooses to face down the threat of German planes, uboats, and artillery to save his countrymen. He votes for certain death, if only in hopes of saving those that would fight for him and his people, despite the warnings given to him by a shellshocked officer of the Royal Army.

He could have stayed home, with his wife and family, and let the Queen's sailors do the job for him. But instead, he rose to the calling of his country, of his people, and told the world he was willing to sacrifice life and limb if only in a fool's gambit. He would throw away everything in hopes of saving those that were in need. Strength, duty, honor, no word is great enough to do his actions the justice they deserve. He embodies the mindset we must all carry in our struggle, our fight for the survival of our people: We must do what we Can, not what we Must.

And lastly, with the pilot Farrier, we see the sacrifice. While most of the movie is spent with beautiful and adrenaline pumping dog-fights, we don't truly see the lesson to be learned by Tom Hardy's character until the end of the movie. With a broken fuel gauge, and only an estimation on the time he has left before his engine fails him and he plummets out of the sky, Farrier faces a moment where he can either save himself and fly back to England with what little fuel he has left, or expend the remaining reservoir and save as many lives as he can from the munitions of a German bomber.

He sacrifices himself, what he thinks is his life, to fight for the lives of his comrades, and chases after the bomber, in hopes of saving whomever he can. Though the German bomber is successful in sinking it's target, eventually the craft is downed. Farrier, discovering his fuel has run out, glides down to the potential safety of the beach, knowing full well he might die down there. He lands safely, and is immediately taken prisoner by the advancing German forces.

He embodies love for one's fellow countrymen. He did what was right in spite of the harm he would face afterwords. He did what he needed in order to ensure that many more could fight on, could live to see another sunrise. He embodied what it meant to sacrifice one's self for a greater cause.

This movie was fantastic. Marvelous, even. Even though we know that there may never be a time when the sacrifices of the German soldiers will be immortalized in film, where the Bravery of the other side of that war will be commemorated, and where the sacrifice of those fighting for the existence and freedom of their people against an indescribable evil will be told in anything outside of a villainous light, I cannot in any way say that this movie did not embody what we, as the beginnings of a movement for the future of our people, should strive for.

No person in the AltRight should refrain from seeing this movie. No child should not be taught it's lessons. The stories of Dunkirk should be an inspiration to us all.

Great points about how the film is focused on us, not them. On courage, sacrifice, honor, and daring, as well as sympathy and understanding to those who deserve it, like the shell-shocked soldier. Seeing noble virtues being taught onscreen like this is rare nowadays. It really highlights the yawning chasm of genuine morality in our popular art.
